title: The Model Isn’t Wrong—You’re Just Bad at Prompting

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is prompt design techniques including Chain of Thought, few-shot, and meta-prompting patterns. The content covers general prompt engineering techniques not tied to any specific application vertical. The discussion centers on crafting and iterating on prompts during feature development. Prerequisites are basic familiarity with LLMs, but nuances around reasoning models and research findings raise it beyond beginner level. This is a recorded conference presentation delivered to an AI engineering audience. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript with character-level evidence anchors.

summary: Dan, co-founder of PromptHub ("the GitHub for prompts"), delivers a comprehensive overview of prompt engineering techniques and their evolving application with reasoning models. He begins by arguing that prompt engineering remains essential—anyone who has shipped AI features knows it is far more nuanced than simply telling the model what to do. He references Anthropic's guidance about starting with the simplest solution, warning against prematurely jumping to complex RAG systems before spending adequate time on prompt refinement, since everyone has access to the same models and prompts plus architecture are where competitive advantage lies. The talk covers two main methods: Chain of Thought (CoT) and Few-Shot prompting. CoT instructs the model to reason through problems before answering, breaking them into sub-problems. Dan explains zero-shot CoT (adding phrases like "think step by step"), few-shot CoT with reasoning examples, and automated frameworks like AutoReason and Auto-CoT. He notes DeepSeek's R1 training template generated reasoning chains within think tags to train the model. For few-shot prompting, Dan explains the "show rather than tell" approach using input-output examples, emphasizing that most performance gains come from just one or two diverse examples and that performance can degrade with too many. Meta prompting—using LLMs to create or refine prompts—is covered with free tools from Anthropic, OpenAI, and PromptHub, the latter tailoring meta-prompts to specific model providers. A significant portion addresses reasoning models (o1, DeepSeek-R1). Dan cites Microsoft's MedPrompt framework paper showing that adding examples degraded o1 performance; DeepSeek researchers found the same; and OpenAI cautioned that extra context can overcomplicate and confuse reasoning models. However, extended reasoning improves output quality—DeepSeek found that as reasoning length increased during training, accuracy improved. For reasoning models, Dan recommends clear task descriptions, encouraging more reasoning for difficult problems, avoiding few-shot prompting (or using at most one or two examples), and not instructing the model on how to reason since it is built in. Dan concludes by sharing free resources including the Prompt Engineering Substack, PromptHub blog, community templates, and reasoning prompt collections.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Agenda
sections.summary: Dan introduces himself as co-founder of PromptHub, a Lakers/LeBron fan and marathon runner. He outlines the talk agenda: why prompt engineering matters, Chain of Thought prompting, few-shot prompting, meta prompting, reasoning model differences, and free templates/resources.

sections.title: Why Prompt Engineering Matters
sections.summary: Dan argues prompt engineering is the most accessible way to improve LLM outputs and provides competitive advantage since everyone has access to the same models. He references Anthropic's guidance to start with the simplest solution and warns against prematurely jumping to complex RAG without first spending time on prompt refinement.

sections.title: Chain of Thought Prompting
sections.summary: Dan explains CoT prompting—having the model reason before answering. He covers zero-shot approaches (e.g., 'think step by step'), few-shot CoT with reasoning examples, and automated frameworks like AutoReason and Auto-CoT. He notes DeepSeek's R1 used think tags to generate reasoning chains for training. Multiple reasoning templates are available free in PromptHub.

sections.title: Few-Shot Prompting
sections.summary: Dan explains few-shot prompting as 'show rather than tell'—providing input-output examples for the model to mimic. He emphasizes most performance gains come from just one or two diverse examples, and performance can degrade with too many examples. Examples should cover different expected input types.

sections.title: Meta Prompting
sections.summary: Dan introduces meta prompting—using LLMs to create, refine, or improve prompts. He mentions frameworks requiring voting knowledge and free tools from Anthropic, OpenAI, and PromptHub. PromptHub's tool tailors meta-prompts to specific model providers and offers a co-pilot iteration experience.

sections.title: Reasoning Models and Prompting Differences
sections.summary: Dan explains reasoning models require different prompting. Microsoft's MedPrompt paper and DeepSeek both found few-shot examples degrade reasoning model performance. OpenAI cautioned extra context can confuse models. However, extended reasoning improves output quality—DeepSeek found reasoning length correlated with accuracy. Recommendations: clear task description, encourage more reasoning, avoid few-shot (or use at most one or two), and do not instruct on how to reason.

sections.title: Resources and Closing
sections.summary: Dan shares free resources: Prompt Engineering Substack, PromptHub blog, community templates and reasoning prompt collections. He closes by thanking the audience.
